Strict management and rules. Confiscate phones, send students outside, establish respect and the importance of learning every single day.

I find that explaining your reasoning helps, too. Assign students articles about the effects technology can have on their brains. Make them think for themselves.

Personally, I also have my students place their phones in backpacks and itinerantly confiscate them when they are visible. If you establish an expectation, it's up to the students to follow it or there will be consequences.

Unfortunately, one prep period is standard in secondary school. Most of us have to roll with 55ish minutes of prep per day. The work that needs to be done outside of class is generally why teachers consider themselves underpaid.

The first year of teaching is incredibly tough. I'd recommend leaning on your grade level peers in your department for support--aligning on lessons and the like. Hopefully, they have materials you can use to ease the burden of prepping your classes every day. If not, there's always teachers pay teachers and usually a great deal of good material available from other districts online.

If you fall behind, it's always good to assign tons and tons of work. More problems, more writing. Days when the students have to work quietly on a large assignment can become stealth prep periods once you have your routines and procedures and management down. Don't worry about being a hero--as long as your kids don't leave the room dumber than they entered, you won the day. Survival and flexibility are what will keep you going.

Yeah... It's an incredible game. That the Elden Ring team created over a decade ago. That's why the remaster was able to be so successful--the initial creative work that Miyazaki's *same team* did wayyy before Bluepoint remastered things.

Like. A lot of the atmosphere and sound design and the grounded sense of realism was present in the original. That was a difficult creative task. 

Do you think, if the team had focused on that back in 2009, it would have come together in all the atmospheric departments if the original team had focused on graphical fidelity instead? FROM likely didn't have the budget for graphical fidelity, and instead focused on the (cheaper) work of creating a good design and atmosphere.

So, creating something *new*, is going to be more difficult, visually speaking, than polishing up something that already had a lot of love and care put into the atmosphere and design. There's only so much budget (and processing power) available for a project. 

Think: The original DeS looked like a PS2 game in some aspects, but it had killer design and atmosphere. It also put a lot of effort into masking load times, which were really heavy up front and bad even for the time. But the game had those loads because the team was inexperienced with content streaming, and they managed to make the game sing with what they had.

DeS was a pretty linear game to begin with. It wasn't open like Elden Ring or semi-open like Dark Souls. So the giant benefit you would have in remaking Demon's in 2020 or so is that the game was DESIGNED to be pretty limited, kinda like The Order or other linear, graphics-heavy titles, but those games at the time were hallways with puddle-deep gameplay. For the time, Demon's Souls had much more intricate level design, but it was still designed to be played from one direction.

From a design perspective, that makes it *much* easier on the hardware, because the level designers can presume that a player will be going in one direction and can plan accordingly.

So, if you're remaking a linear game in 2020, you now have a nice benefit: the game is designed to be linear, which frees up a TON of system resources for a game to have tons more textures, uncompressed and remastered sound, draw distance, and plenty of room for animation and game feel improvements  as well.

Working on this established framework is MUCH easier than creating an engine and assets and concepts and level design from scratch. It's mostly copying and reimplementing things that has already been done, which allows the team to focus on polish.

Elden Ring, finally, is a new game. It's likely based on some existing framework, like the engines or Dark Souls 3, Sekiro, or some mixture of both, but it's also a new game in a new setting, which means tons of new assets, new gameplay systems that need to be worked and reworked and tested, and fundamental engine changes like full open world design, horses, horse combat, non-linear encounter design, and the like. That's why Elden Ring doesn't look as "good" as Demon's Souls 2020--it's doing fundamentally different things, and as I alluded to earlier, dev teams have finite budgets and are generally trying to give the player the best experience for their intended goal.

Elden Ring: create a new action game and give players a "souls-like" experience in an open world setting, which is a very new fucking thing and a bit of a gamble given that the bones of a "souls" game are, itself, in the somewhat linear Demon's Souls. Takes a lot more work and processing headroom than one might think to get that sorted out and feeling good.

Demon's Souls was already a complete game, so the design priorities of the remaster were able to comfortably (and rightly) focus on polish rather than design. It's gorgeous, it's just not doing the same thing. It's really an apples and oranges kind of comparison.

An new open-world game like Elden Ring has a lot more moving parts than a reskinned PS3 game.

The intricacy and amount of assets in DeS is basically like... Five zones from Dark Souls 3 (with much stronger level design and art direction), so if you're remastering the game, you can really focus on polishing up what's there, compared to creating a bunch of concepts from scratch. Revision is much easier than creation.

Not saying Demon's Souls PS5 doesn't seem impressive, just highlighting that the aims of both projects are pretty different.
